segments.text: Mark stands in line at a coffee shop.
His hands are sweaty. His heart beats fast.
Behind him, a man with a friendly smile waits. The man is a tourist. He looks lost. He taps Mark on the shoulder. "Excuse me," the man says. "Do
you speak English?"
Mark turns around.
His mouth opens. His brain knows the words. "Yes, I speak English. How can I help you?" But nothing comes out. His throat feels tight. His mind goes blank.
The man waits. Mark's face turns red. He nods. He points at the menu. He makes a strange sound.
Uh the man smiles politely and walks away. Mark stands there feeling small, feeling stupid,

feeling like all those years of studying meant nothing. Has this ever happened to you? Yes, of course it has. Because you're human, and this is what happens when your brain forgets English the moment you need it most.
Let's rewind.
Let's look at Mark's life.
Mark studies English every day. He has notebooks full of vocabulary. He knows the grammar rules.
He can pass tests. He watches English videos.
He reads English
articles.
He does everything right, but there's a problem. A big problem. Mark practices English like he's learning to play the piano by reading sheet music.
He knows all the notes.
He knows where they go on the page, but he's never actually played the piano. Then, one day, someone asks him to perform, and his fingers freeze.
Because reading
about music and making music are two completely different things.
This is exactly what happens with English.
Mark learns words in isolation. He learns
rules. He learns translations.
But he never practices using English in real situations.
He never practices the feeling of being in a conversation. He never trains his brain to find words
under pressure. And then, when the moment comes, his brain doesn't forget the words. It panics.
And when your brain panics, it shuts down. That's not a language problem. That's a survival problem. Let me explain.
There's a part
of your brain called the amygdala. It's small, it's shaped like an almond, and its job is to protect you from danger.
When you feel threatened, the amygdala takes over. It doesn't care about English. It doesn't care about grammar.
It doesn't care about sounding smart. It only cares about one thing, survival.
Your amygdala is like a security guard.
It's always watching, always ready to act. When you're alone in your room studying English, the security guard is relaxed. Nothing dangerous here, it thinks. Go ahead, practice your verbs.

But when you're face-to-face with a native speaker, the security guard wakes up. Wait, it says. This is a social situation. This is high pressure. I don't know this person. What if I make a mistake? What if I look stupid? What if
they laugh at me? And just like that, the amygdala sounds the alarm. It sends a message to your brain, "Danger!
Shut down everything!" And your brain listens.
It stops thinking about words.

It stops thinking about grammar. It focuses on one thing, getting out of this situation safely. That's why you freeze. That's why you forget. That's why you feel like you don't know anything. Because your brain is trying
to protect you from something it thinks is dangerous. Here's the thing, speaking English is not dangerous. You're not going to get hurt. You're not going to die. Your brain just doesn't know that.

It's overprotective. It's scared, and it needs to learn that conversations are safe. Think about driving a car. The first time you drove, you were terrified. Your hands shook. Your heart raced. You forgot where the pedals were.
Now, you drive without thinking, because your brain learned that driving is safe.

The same thing happens with English. You need to teach your brain that speaking English is not a threat. So, how do you do that? Simple. You practice the thing that scares you, but you practice it in a way that doesn't trigger the panic.
Here are three simple actions. Each one takes less than five minutes. Each one will change how your brain responds to English. You can start today, right now.
The five-second warm-up.
Before any conversation, take five seconds. Close your eyes. Breathe in deeply. Exhale slowly. Then, say this to yourself, "I
am safe. This is just practice. Mistakes don't matter."
This sounds silly, but it works.
Because you're telling your amygdala to calm down.
You're telling your security guard, "False alarm.
Everything's fine.
Go back to sleep."
Do this every time. Before meetings, before phone calls, before ordering coffee.
Train your brain that conversations are not emergencies. Action two, the safe words exercise. Choose five phrases.
Very simple phrases. Phrases you can say without thinking. For Mark, it might be, "That's interesting. Could you repeat that? I'm sorry. I didn't catch that.
Let me think about that. That's a good question."
Practice these phrases until they feel automatic. Now, when you freeze, you have something to say. Even if your brain goes blank, you can use
one of these phrases. That buys you time. It stops the panic from growing.
It gives your brain a chance to find the words you actually need. Action three, the morning voice practice.
Every morning, spend three minutes talking to yourself. Out loud in English.
Talk
about anything. What am I doing today?
How do I feel? What happened yesterday?
This trains your brain to produce English without fear. It normalizes speaking.
It reduces the pressure.
When you're comfortable talking to yourself, you'll be more comfortable talking to others. These actions are small. They're
easy, but they change everything.
Because they don't teach you more words.
They teach your brain to use the words you already know. Let's go back to Mark.

Three weeks later, different coffee shop, same situation. A foreigner approaches. "Excuse me, do you speak English?" Mark's heart starts to race, but then he remembers. He takes a breath, he closes his eyes for 1 second.
"I am safe," he thinks. "This is just practice." He opens his eyes, he smiles.
"Yes, I do," he says. "How can I help you?" The foreigner looks relieved. "Oh, thank you.
I need directions to the museum." Mark's brain searches for the words, and this time they appear slowly, carefully, but they appear. "The museum
is two streets from here," Mark says.
"You go straight, then turn left at the big church." The foreigner smiles.

"Thank you so much." "You're welcome," Mark says. He didn't speak perfectly. He made small mistakes, but he spoke, and that's what matters. Mark walks away from that coffee shop with a smile. He didn't become fluent overnight, he
didn't become a native speaker.
He just did one thing differently. He taught his brain that conversations are safe, and that made all the difference. If you've ever frozen in a conversation, if you've
ever forgotten basic words, if you've ever felt like you'll never be fluent, you are not failing. You are not stupid.
Your brain is just trying to protect you from something it doesn't understand.
But now, you understand, and now you can change.
You have the tools, you have the knowledge, and you have Mark. He's not perfect, he never will be, but he's brave, and so are you. Here's my
question for you. When was the last time you froze in an English conversation?

And what do you wish you would have said? Write it in the comments. Share your story. Mark wants to hear it, and I want to help you. Remember, English is not about being perfect, it's about being brave enough to try. Join Mark
next time for another lesson. Subscribe now, and let's keep practicing together.
See you soon.
